claim: Mitochondria harbor an independent genome called mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which contains essential metabolic genes.
source: Mitochondria harbor an independent genome, called mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which contains essential metabolic genes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about mitochondria and mtDNA.

claim: mtDNA mutations occur at high frequency.
source: Although mtDNA mutations occur at high frequency, they are inherited infrequently, indicating that germline mechanisms limit their accumulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and is cited in the introduction.

claim: mtDNA mutations are inherited infrequently.
source: Although mtDNA mutations occur at high frequency, they are inherited infrequently, indicating that germline mechanisms limit their accumulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and is cited in the introduction.

claim: Germline mechanisms limit the accumulation of mtDNA mutations.
source: Although mtDNA mutations occur at high frequency, they are inherited infrequently, indicating that germline mechanisms limit their accumulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutations occur frequently but are inherited infrequently.

claim: C. elegans PGCs combine strategies to generate a low point in mtDNA number by segregating mitochondria into lobe-like protrusions that are cannibalized by adjacent cells.
source: We show that PGCs combine strategies to generate a low point in mtDNA number by segregating mitochondria into lobe-like protrusions that are cannibalized by adjacent cells, and by concurrently eliminating mitochondria through autophagy, reducing overall mtDNA content twofold.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: C. elegans PGCs eliminate mitochondria through autophagy.
source: We show that PGCs combine strategies to generate a low point in mtDNA number by segregating mitochondria into lobe-like protrusions that are cannibalized by adjacent cells, and by concurrently eliminating mitochondria through autophagy, reducing overall mtDNA content twofold.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lobe cannibalism and autophagy reduce overall mtDNA content in PGCs twofold.
source: We show that PGCs combine strategies to generate a low point in mtDNA number by segregating mitochondria into lobe-like protrusions that are cannibalized by adjacent cells, and by concurrently eliminating mitochondria through autophagy, reducing overall mtDNA content twofold.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: As PGCs exit quiescence and divide, mtDNAs replicate to maintain a set point of ~200 mtDNAs per germline stem cell.
source: As PGCs exit quiescence and divide, mtDNAs replicate to maintain a set point of ~200 mtDNAs per germline stem cell.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cannibalism and autophagy eliminate mtDNAs stochastically.
source: Whereas cannibalism and autophagy eliminate mtDNAs stochastically, we show that the kinase PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1), operating independently of Parkin and autophagy, preferentially reduces the fraction of mutant mtDNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PINK1, operating independently of Parkin and autophagy, preferentially reduces the fraction of mutant mtDNAs.
source: Whereas cannibalism and autophagy eliminate mtDNAs stochastically, we show that the kinase PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1), operating independently of Parkin and autophagy, preferentially reduces the fraction of mutant mtDNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PGCs employ parallel mechanisms to control both the quantity and quality of the founding population of germline mtDNAs.
source: Thus, PGCs employ parallel mechanisms to control both the quantity and quality of the founding population of germline mtDNAs.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: mtDNA has a high mutation rate compared to nuclear DNA.
source: Compared to nuclear DNA, mtDNA has a high mutation rate and is repaired inefficiently (Fu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2020.

claim: mtDNA is repaired inefficiently compared to nuclear DNA.
source: Compared to nuclear DNA, mtDNA has a high mutation rate and is repaired inefficiently (Fu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2020.

claim: Deleterious mtDNA mutations can lead to mitochondrial disease if present at sufficiently high heteroplasmy.
source: Deleterious mtDNA mutations can lead to mitochondrial disease if present at sufficiently high heteroplasmy – a condition that is estimated to affect ~1 in 5000 individuals and has no known cure (Gorman et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gorman et al., 2015.

claim: Mitochondrial disease is estimated to affect ~1 in 5000 individuals.
source: Deleterious mtDNA mutations can lead to mitochondrial disease if present at sufficiently high heteroplasmy – a condition that is estimated to affect ~1 in 5000 individuals and has no known cure (Gorman et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gorman et al., 2015.

claim: Mitochondrial disease has no known cure.
source: Deleterious mtDNA mutations can lead to mitochondrial disease if present at sufficiently high heteroplasmy – a condition that is estimated to affect ~1 in 5000 individuals and has no known cure (Gorman et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gorman et al., 2015.

claim: Embryos inherit their mtDNAs exclusively from the pool present within the oocyte.
source: However, embryos inherit their mtDNAs exclusively from the pool present within the oocyte (Palozzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Palozzi et al., 2018.

claim: Relatively few deleterious mtDNA mutations are transmitted over generations.
source: However, relatively few deleterious mutations are transmitted over generations (Nachman, 1998), indicating that mtDNA mutations are selected against within the germ line.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nachman, 1998.

claim: mtDNA mutations are selected against within the germ line.
source: However, relatively few deleterious mutations are transmitted over generations (Nachman, 1998), indicating that mtDNA mutations are selected against within the germ line.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that few deleterious mutations are transmitted over generations, as cited from Nachman, 1998.

claim: In vertebrates, a bottleneck occurs in embryonic primordial germ cells (PGCs) due to the dilution of maternally provided mtDNAs by reductive embryonic cell divisions, or via the replication of a subset of mtDNA genomes in PGCs.
source: In vertebrates, a bottleneck occurs in embryonic primordial germ cells (PGCs) due to the dilution of maternally provided mtDNAs by reductive embryonic cell divisions, or via the replication of a subset of mtDNA genomes in PGCs (Cao et al., 2007; Cree et al., 2008; Floros et al., 2018; Jenuth et al., 1996; Otten et al., 2016; Wai et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The entire C. elegans germ line descends from two PGCs.
source: The entire C. elegans germ line descends from two PGCs, which are born early in embryogenesis and remain quiescent until early larval stages (Fukuyama et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fukuyama et al., 2006.

claim: C. elegans PGCs are born early in embryogenesis and remain quiescent until early larval stages.
source: The entire C. elegans germ line descends from two PGCs, which are born early in embryogenesis and remain quiescent until early larval stages (Fukuyama et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fukuyama et al., 2006.

claim: Embryonic PGCs do not divide.
source: Although embryonic PGCs do not divide, they undergo a non-mitotic cellular remodeling process, discarding much of their cell mass and content.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about C. elegans PGCs.

claim: Embryonic PGCs undergo a non-mitotic cellular remodeling process, discarding much of their cell mass and content.
source: Although embryonic PGCs do not divide, they undergo a non-mitotic cellular remodeling process, discarding much of their cell mass and content.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about C. elegans PGCs.

claim: PGC remodeling occurs when PGCs form organelle-filled lobe-like protrusions, which adjacent endodermal cells cannibalize and digest.
source: Remodeling occurs when PGCs form organelle-filled lobe-like protrusions, which adjacent endodermal cells cannibalize and digest (Figure 1A; Abdu et al., 2016; Sulston et al., 1983).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Abdu et al., 2016 and Sulston et al., 1983, and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: PGCs lose much of their mitochondrial mass in the process of lobe cannibalism.
source: Previously, we showed that PGCs lose much of their mitochondrial mass in the process of lobe cannibalism, suggesting that one role of this remodeling event could be to eliminate PGC mitochondria in bulk (Abdu et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Abdu et al., 2016.

claim: Most PGC mitochondria moved into lobes shortly after they formed.
source: Most PGC mitochondria moved into lobes shortly after they formed (Figure 1B–C) but a subset returned to the cell body prior to lobe digestion (Figure 1D and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: A subset of PGC mitochondria returned to the cell body prior to lobe digestion.
source: Most PGC mitochondria moved into lobes shortly after they formed (Figure 1B–C) but a subset returned to the cell body prior to lobe digestion (Figure 1D and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 1D, F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Cell body mitochondria that are retained in L1 PGCs represent the founding population present at the onset of larval germline expansion.
source: Cell body mitochondria that are retained in L1 PGCs (Figure 1E) represent the founding population present at the onset of larval germline expansion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PGC lobe fragments present within endodermal cells colocalize with the lysosomal marker LAMP-1.
source: The PGC lobe fragments present within endodermal cells colocalize with the lysosomal marker LAMP-1, suggesting that mitochondria within lobes are targeted for destruction and digested (Abdu et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Abdu et al., 2016.

claim: Mitochondria within lobes are targeted for destruction and digested.
source: The PGC lobe fragments present within endodermal cells colocalize with the lysosomal marker LAMP-1, suggesting that mitochondria within lobes are targeted for destruction and digested (Abdu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization with LAMP-1, as cited from Abdu et al., 2016.

claim: Mito-DendraPGC fluorescence was greatly reduced in cannibalized lobe mitochondria compared to pH-insensitive Mito-mChPGC in L1 larvae.
source: In L1 larvae, Mito-DendraPGC fluorescence was greatly reduced in cannibalized lobe mitochondria compared to pH-insensitive Mito-mChPGC (Shaner et al., 2004; arrowheads, Figure 1G–H), whereas both markers labeled PGC cell body mitochondria robustly (dashed outline, Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Both Mito-DendraPGC and Mito-mChPGC labeled PGC cell body mitochondria robustly.
source: In L1 larvae, Mito-DendraPGC fluorescence was greatly reduced in cannibalized lobe mitochondria compared to pH-insensitive Mito-mChPGC (Shaner et al., 2004; arrowheads, Figure 1G–H), whereas both markers labeled PGC cell body mitochondria robustly (dashed outline, Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: PGC lobe mitochondria are digested by endodermal cells shortly after lobes are cannibalized.
source: We conclude that PGC lobe mitochondria are digested by endodermal cells shortly after lobes are cannibalized, permanently removing them from the mitochondrial pool passed on to L1 larval PGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PGC lobe mitochondria are permanently removed from the mitochondrial pool passed on to L1 larval PGCs.
source: We conclude that PGC lobe mitochondria are digested by endodermal cells shortly after lobes are cannibalized, permanently removing them from the mitochondrial pool passed on to L1 larval PGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In human cells, individual TFAM nucleoids appear as puncta within the mitochondrial matrix and contain single, or at most a few, mtDNA genomes.
source: In human cells, individual TFAM nucleoids appear as puncta within the mitochondrial matrix and contain single, or at most a few, mtDNA genomes (Brown et al., 2011; Kukat et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2011 and Kukat et al., 2011.

claim: TFAM-GFP protein was expressed ubiquitously and formed puncta that localized to mitochondria.
source: The TFAM-GFP protein was expressed ubiquitously and formed puncta that localized to mitochondria, consistent with its known binding to mtDNA in C. elegans (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B and cited from Yang et al., 2022.

claim: TFAM-GFP puncta were present in both cell body and lobe mitochondria, including those that had been recently cannibalized.
source: Within PGCs, TFAM-GFP puncta were present in both cell body and lobe mitochondria, including those that had been recently cannibalized (arrowhead, Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The number of TFAM-GFP foci decreased more than twofold between embryogenesis and the L1 larval stage.
source: The number of TFAM-GFP foci decreased more than twofold between embryogenesis and the L1 larval stage (Figure 1J–L), suggesting that lobe cannibalism results in a substantial loss of PGC mtDNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 1J-L.

claim: Lobe cannibalism results in a substantial loss of PGC mtDNAs.
source: The number of TFAM-GFP foci decreased more than twofold between embryogenesis and the L1 larval stage (Figure 1J–L), suggesting that lobe cannibalism results in a substantial loss of PGC mtDNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TFAM-GFP foci decreased more than twofold between embryogenesis and the L1 larval stage.

claim: Each embryonic PGC contained 401 ± 11 mtDNAs.
source: We determined that each embryonic PGC contained 401 ± 11 mtDNAs (Figure 2B), which is 1.2% of the number of mtDNAs we detected in whole early embryos (33,840 ± 1784) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Whole early embryos contain 33,840 ± 1784 mtDNAs.
source: We determined that each embryonic PGC contained 401 ± 11 mtDNAs (Figure 2B), which is 1.2% of the number of mtDNAs we detected in whole early embryos (33,840 ± 1784) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The volume of each embryonic PGC in vivo is 275 ± 7.2 µm3.
source: The volume of each embryonic PGC in vivo (275 ± 7.2 µm3) is 1.2% of the volume of whole embryos (23,949 ± 175 µm3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that embryonic PGCs inherit their mtDNAs from the pool present at fertilization through reductive embryonic cell divisions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The volume of whole embryos is 23,949 ± 175 µm3.
source: The volume of each embryonic PGC in vivo (275 ± 7.2 µm3) is 1.2% of the volume of whole embryos (23,949 ± 175 µm3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that embryonic PGCs inherit their mtDNAs from the pool present at fertilization through reductive embryonic cell divisions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Embryonic PGCs inherit their mtDNAs from the pool present at fertilization through reductive embryonic cell divisions.
source: The volume of each embryonic PGC in vivo (275 ± 7.2 µm3) is 1.2% of the volume of whole embryos (23,949 ± 175 µm3) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that embryonic PGCs inherit their mtDNAs from the pool present at fertilization through reductive embryonic cell divisions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the volume of embryonic PGCs is 1.2% of the volume of whole embryos, which matches the proportion of mtDNAs.

claim: Late embryonic PGCs, which lacked lobes, contained only 272 ± 8.1 mtDNAs.
source: By contrast, late embryonic PGCs, which lacked lobes, contained only 272 ± 8.1 mtDNAs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Sorted L1 larval PGCs contained 220 ± 12 mtDNAs.
source: Sorted L1 larval PGCs contained even fewer mtDNAs (220 ± 12; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PGC lobe cannibalism could eliminate a third of the mtDNA molecules that each PGC inherits at its birth.
source: Together, these data suggest that PGC lobe cannibalism could eliminate a third of the mtDNA molecules that each PGC inherits at its birth, and that an additional mechanism further reduces mtDNA numbers between late embryogenesis and the L1 larval stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An additional mechanism further reduces mtDNA numbers between late embryogenesis and the L1 larval stage.
source: Together, these data suggest that PGC lobe cannibalism could eliminate a third of the mtDNA molecules that each PGC inherits at its birth, and that an additional mechanism further reduces mtDNA numbers between late embryogenesis and the L1 larval stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Each PGC in the larval germ line contains roughly half the number of mtDNAs that they inherit during embryogenesis.
source: Thus, each PGC in the larval germ line contains roughly half the number that they inherit during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most PGCs fail to form lobes in nop-1 mutants.
source: To directly test whether lobe cannibalism contributes to the loss of mtDNAs in PGCs, we examined PGC mtDNA number in nop-1 mutants, in which most PGCs fail to form lobes (Figure 2C–D; Maniscalco et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Maniscalco et al., 2020 and data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: nop-1 mutant L1 PGCs retained a significantly higher proportion of embryonic PGC mtDNAs compared to wild type.
source: The nop-1 mutant L1 PGCs retained a significantly higher proportion of embryonic PGC mtDNAs compared to wild type (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2E and G.

claim: Lobe cannibalism contributes to the reduction in mtDNA that occurs as PGCs transition from embryogenesis to the L1 stage.
source: This finding implicates lobe cannibalism in the reduction in mtDNA that occurs as PGCs transition from embryogenesis to the L1 stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: One or more large, distinct foci of acidified mitochondria were observed within many PGCs prior to lobe cannibalism.
source: We observed one or more large, distinct foci of acidified mitochondria [mCherry(+) Dendra(-)] within many PGCs prior to lobe cannibalism (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and foci were absent in autophagy-defective atg-18/WD repeat domain phosphoinositide interacting 2 (WIPI2) mutants (see Figure 5F–G; Palmisano and Meléndez, 2019), suggesting that autophagy may be responsible for lobe-independent degradation of mtDNA in PGCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Acidified mitochondria foci were absent in autophagy-defective atg-18 mutants.
source: We observed one or more large, distinct foci of acidified mitochondria [mCherry(+) Dendra(-)] within many PGCs prior to lobe cannibalism (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and foci were absent in autophagy-defective atg-18/WD repeat domain phosphoinositide interacting 2 (WIPI2) mutants (see Figure 5F–G; Palmisano and Meléndez, 2019), suggesting that autophagy may be responsible for lobe-independent degradation of mtDNA in PGCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 5F-G and cited from Palmisano and Meléndez, 2019.

claim: Autophagy may be responsible for lobe-independent degradation of mtDNA in PGCs.
source: We observed one or more large, distinct foci of acidified mitochondria [mCherry(+) Dendra(-)] within many PGCs prior to lobe cannibalism (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and foci were absent in autophagy-defective atg-18/WD repeat domain phosphoinositide interacting 2 (WIPI2) mutants (see Figure 5F–G; Palmisano and Meléndez, 2019), suggesting that autophagy may be responsible for lobe-independent degradation of mtDNA in PGCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that acidified mitochondria foci were absent in autophagy-defective mutants.

claim: mtDNA reduction was entirely prevented in nop-1; atg-18 L1 PGCs.
source: Notably, mtDNA reduction was entirely prevented in nop-1; atg-18 L1 PGCs, which inherited a larger proportion of embryonic PGC mtDNAs than nop-1 single mutants (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2E and G.

claim: nop-1; atg-18 L1 PGCs inherited a larger proportion of embryonic PGC mtDNAs than nop-1 single mutants.
source: Notably, mtDNA reduction was entirely prevented in nop-1; atg-18 L1 PGCs, which inherited a larger proportion of embryonic PGC mtDNAs than nop-1 single mutants (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2E and G.

claim: Lobe cannibalism and autophagy are both required for complete mtDNA copy number reduction in PGCs.
source: Together, these results (and data below; see Figure 5A–B) suggest that lobe cannibalism and autophagy are both required for complete mtDNA copy number reduction in PGCs, and indicate that if any mtDNA replication occurs in late embryonic or L1 PGCs, it is insufficient to outpace autophagy-mediated mitochondrial destruction at this stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: If any mtDNA replication occurs in late embryonic or L1 PGCs, it is insufficient to outpace autophagy-mediated mitochondrial destruction at this stage.
source: Together, these results (and data below; see Figure 5A–B) suggest that lobe cannibalism and autophagy are both required for complete mtDNA copy number reduction in PGCs, and indicate that if any mtDNA replication occurs in late embryonic or L1 PGCs, it is insufficient to outpace autophagy-mediated mitochondrial destruction at this stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Changing TFAM activity can alter mtDNA copy number.
source: To distinguish between these possibilities, we took advantage of the fact that changing TFAM activity can alter mtDNA copy number (Larsson et al., 1998; Sumitani et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Larsson et al., 1998 and Sumitani et al., 2011.

claim: Whole embryos from the TFAM-GFP knock-in strain contained significantly fewer mtDNAs (8450 ± 768) than wild type.
source: Indeed, we found that whole embryos from the TFAM-GFP knock-in strain contained significantly fewer mtDNAs (8450 ± 768) than wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), indicating that the GFP tag partially interferes with TFAM function.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The GFP tag partially interferes with TFAM function.
source: Indeed, we found that whole embryos from the TFAM-GFP knock-in strain contained significantly fewer mtDNAs (8450 ± 768) than wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), indicating that the GFP tag partially interferes with TFAM function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TFAM-GFP embryos contain significantly fewer mtDNAs than wild type.

claim: TFAM-GFP embryonic PGCs contained 89 ± 3 mtDNAs.
source: The TFAM-GFP embryonic PGCs contained 89 ± 3 mtDNAs and TFAM-GFP L1 PGCs contained 54 ± 2 mtDNAs (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TFAM-GFP L1 PGCs contained 54 ± 2 mtDNAs.
source: The TFAM-GFP embryonic PGCs contained 89 ± 3 mtDNAs and TFAM-GFP L1 PGCs contained 54 ± 2 mtDNAs (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: L1 PGCs inherit a comparable percentage of the mtDNAs contained within embryonic PGCs in both wild-type (55%) and TFAM-GFP (60%) strains.
source: Thus, despite the presence of markedly fewer mtDNAs in the TFAM-GFP strain, L1 PGCs still inherit a comparable percentage of the mtDNAs contained within embryonic PGCs (wild-type: 55% and TFAM-GFP: 60%; Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: When embryonic PGCs contained ~25% excess mtDNAs (in the mptDf2 mtDNA mutant strain), a twofold reduction in mtDNAs was still observed by the L1 stage.
source: Conversely, when embryonic PGCs contained ~25% excess mtDNAs (in the mptDf2 mtDNA mutant strain), we still observed a twofold reduction in mtDNAs by the L1 stage (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Lobe cannibalism and autophagy do not subtract the number of PGC mtDNAs to a defined number, but rather divide the population of PGC mtDNAs present by a fixed proportion.
source: Together, these data indicate that lobe cannibalism and autophagy do not subtract the number of PGC mtDNAs to a defined number, but rather divide the population of PGC mtDNAs present by a fixed proportion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When L1 larvae first encounter food, PGCs exit from quiescence and begin to proliferate, forming a population of undifferentiated germline stem cells (GSCs).
source: When L1 larvae first encounter food, PGCs exit from quiescence and begin to proliferate, forming a population of undifferentiated germline stem cells (GSCs) (Fukuyama et al., 2006; Hubbard and Schedl, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fukuyama et al., 2006 and Hubbard and Schedl, 2019.

claim: Previous qPCR experiments on whole worms first revealed a significant expansion of germline mtDNAs after the L3 larval stage.
source: Previous quantitative PCR (qPCR) experiments on whole worms first revealed a significant expansion of germline mtDNAs after the L3 larval stage (Bratic et al., 2009; Tsang and Lemire, 2002a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bratic et al., 2009 and Tsang and Lemire, 2002a.

claim: Larvae fed beginning at the L1 stage showed a progressive increase in the number of TFAM-GFP11 foci per germ line.
source: Larvae fed beginning at the L1 stage showed a progressive increase in the number of TFAM-GFP11 foci per germ line (Figure 3C–F, compare with Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: TFAM-GFP11 foci numbers began to increase even before the first division of the PGCs was complete (early-L1).
source: The TFAM-GFP11 foci numbers began to increase even before the first division of the PGCs was complete (early-L1, Figure 3C and G), and continued to expand through the L2 stage (an average of 22 GSCs), when we stopped our analysis (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 3C and G.

claim: TFAM-GFP11 foci continued to expand through the L2 stage (an average of 22 GSCs).
source: The TFAM-GFP11 foci numbers began to increase even before the first division of the PGCs was complete (early-L1, Figure 3C and G), and continued to expand through the L2 stage (an average of 22 GSCs), when we stopped our analysis (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: The number of TFAM-GFP11 foci per germ cell remained constant after a transient spike in early-L1s (two cells), and stabilized at a number of foci similar to that of L1 that had not been fed.
source: In contrast to the increasing number of TFAM-GFP11 foci per germ line over this period, the number of foci per germ cell remained constant after a transient spike in early-L1s (two cells), and stabilized at a number of foci similar to that of L1 that had not been fed (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The number of mtDNAs per germ line increased from mid-L1 to L2 larvae.
source: Consistent with our TFAM-GFP11 observations, the number of mtDNAs per germ line increased over this period (Figure 3I), although the number of mtDNAs per GSC remained constant and similar to that in starved L1s (~200; Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The number of mtDNAs per GSC remained constant and similar to that in starved L1s (~200).
source: Consistent with our TFAM-GFP11 observations, the number of mtDNAs per germ line increased over this period (Figure 3I), although the number of mtDNAs per GSC remained constant and similar to that in starved L1s (~200; Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: mtDNAs replicate in bulk as L1 PGCs begin to divide to form GSCs.
source: Together, these results indicate that mtDNAs replicate in bulk as L1 PGCs begin to divide to form GSCs, and thereafter balance mtDNA replication with cell division to maintain a constant number of mtDNAs per GSC, through at least the L2 stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GSCs balance mtDNA replication with cell division to maintain a constant number of mtDNAs per GSC, through at least the L2 stage.
source: Together, these results indicate that mtDNAs replicate in bulk as L1 PGCs begin to divide to form GSCs, and thereafter balance mtDNA replication with cell division to maintain a constant number of mtDNAs per GSC, through at least the L2 stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: nop-1 GSCs isolated from mid-L1 and -L2 larvae contained a similar number of mtDNAs as did wild-type GSCs (~200).
source: Remarkably, nop-1 GSCs isolated from mid-L1 and -L2 larvae contained a similar number of mtDNAs as did wild-type GSCs (~200; Figure 3K–L).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in Figure 3K-L.

claim: GSCs actively coordinate mtDNA replication with cell division to maintain ~200 mtDNA per cell, even if excess mtDNAs are present at the onset of germline expansion.
source: These results suggest that GSCs actively coordinate mtDNA replication with cell division to maintain ~200 mtDNA per cell, even if excess mtDNAs are present at the onset of germline expansion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The uaDf5 deletion removes 3.1 kb of the mitochondrial genome, including several essential genes.
source: The uaDf5 deletion removes 3.1 kb of the mitochondrial genome, including several essential genes (Figure 4A), and therefore can exist only when in heteroplasmy with wild-type mtDNA (Tsang and Lemire, 2002b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tsang and Lemire, 2002b and is illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: uaDf5 can exist only when in heteroplasmy with wild-type mtDNA.
source: The uaDf5 deletion removes 3.1 kb of the mitochondrial genome, including several essential genes (Figure 4A), and therefore can exist only when in heteroplasmy with wild-type mtDNA (Tsang and Lemire, 2002b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tsang and Lemire, 2002b.

claim: uaDf5 persists stably because it is preferentially replicated compared with wild-type mtDNA.
source: However, uaDf5 persists stably because it is preferentially replicated compared with wild-type mtDNA (Yang et al., 2022; Gitschlag et al., 2016; Gitschlag et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2022; Gitschlag et al., 2016; Gitschlag et al., 2020; and Lin et al., 2016.
